ideas.title: Agent Framework Scaffolder
ideas.summary: Paste a task description and instantly get scaffold code side-by-side for LangGraph, CrewAI, and the Claude Agents SDK, with color-coded highlights of each framework's structural idioms.
ideas.description: A browser-based tool where you paste a natural-language task description and instantly see scaffold code generated side-by-side for LangGraph, CrewAI, and the Claude Agents SDK. The scaffolds highlight structural idioms unique to each framework, making it easy to pick the right one without reading three separate docs. No code runs in-browser (keeping it fast and cost-free beyond one API call).
keyFeatures: Text input for task description, instant tabbed scaffold output
Color-coded diff view highlighting framework-specific idioms (loops, tools, memory, handoffs)
One-click copy to clipboard per framework
Optional 'explain this scaffold' sidebar using Claude API
ideas.techStack: React + Vite + Tailwind, Claude API (claude-sonnet-5 for generation)
ideas.whyInteresting: Developers spend hours reading framework docs before committing to one; this compresses that decision to minutes and is a natural classroom demo for teaching agentic architecture patterns.
ideas.inspiredBy: JetBrains blog 'Top Agentic Frameworks for Building Applications 2026' and GitHub trending AI agent repositories https://blog.jetbrains.com/pycharm/2026/06/top-agentic-frameworks-for-building-applications-2026/

ideas.title: Prompt History Grader
ideas.summary: Students upload their exported AI conversation history alongside a project submission; the tool scores prompt quality, iteration, and comprehension signals and generates a structured grading report for professors.
ideas.description: A Flask web app where students upload their exported AI conversation history (Claude JSON export, ChatGPT ZIP, or raw text) alongside their project submission. The tool uses the Claude API to analyze the conversation, scoring for prompt specificity, productive iteration, critical pushback on AI suggestions, and evidence the student understood the output. Professors receive a structured report with scores and supporting excerpts.
keyFeatures: Parses Claude, ChatGPT, and generic JSON conversation export formats
Rubric-based scoring: prompt specificity, iteration quality, comprehension signals, originality
Side-by-side timeline view: conversation history vs. final artifact
Exportable grading report (PDF + JSON) for LMS upload
ideas.techStack: Flask + Claude API, React or Jinja2 frontend, Supabase for storage, pdfkit for report generation
ideas.whyInteresting: As AI-assisted coding becomes the norm, grading only the final output misses how students actually learned; this tool gives professors a practical way to assess the process without requiring real-time surveillance.
ideas.inspiredBy: HN 'Ask HN: What are you working on? June 2026' discussions about assessing AI-assisted student work https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48528779

ideas.title: Video Scene Question Bank
ideas.summary: Students build an app that fetches a YouTube video's chapters and key frames, analyzes them with a vision model, and auto-generates a shareable multiple-choice quiz exportable to Canvas, Google Forms, or Markdown.
ideas.description: Students build a full-stack web app that takes any educational YouTube video, extracts key frames at chapter boundaries using the YouTube Data API, feeds them through a vision-capable model (Claude or Gemini), and auto-generates a multiple-choice question bank from the visual and transcript content. The final product is a shareable quiz that professors can embed in their LMS.
keyFeatures: YouTube URL input: auto-fetches chapters, transcript, and key frame thumbnails
Vision model analysis of frames to identify diagrams, code snippets, and equations
Auto-generated multiple-choice and short-answer questions with answer keys
Export to Canvas quiz XML, Google Forms JSON, or plain Markdown
ideas.techStack: React + Vite, Flask API, YouTube Data API, Claude API (vision) or Gemini API (vision), Supabase
ideas.whyInteresting: It combines API integration, vision AI, and LMS tooling into one project with immediate real-world utility for any professor who records lectures or assigns video homework.
ideas.inspiredBy: MiniMax M3 and Kimi-K2.6 multimodal open-source models released June 2026 with native video and image understanding https://www.devflokers.com/blog/open-source-ai-roundup-june-2026

ideas.title: LLM-Driven Misconception Clustering for CS1 Feedback
ideas.summary: Build an LLM-powered pipeline that classifies and clusters student programming errors by underlying conceptual cause, then generates targeted feedback messages tied to specific misconceptions rather than raw test failures.
ideas.description: Most automated feedback systems (including Jolly Feedback) report what failed, not why. This research extends a SIGCSE 2026 real-time misconception detection framework by applying it offline to archived submission logs, constructing a reusable misconception taxonomy for introductory CS (C++/Java), and then wiring that taxonomy into a targeted LLM critique layer. The system pairs static analysis output from existing autograders with a misconception classifier to produce feedback that names the conceptual gap and suggests a conceptual next step without revealing the answer. This addresses the open question from Pisan's prior work: does misconception-targeted critique reduce resubmission cycles compared to plain pass/fail output?

papers.title: AI-Augmented Instruction: Real-Time Misconception Detection
papers.authors: Georgia Institute of Technology (authors not parsed from poster format)
papers.abstract: We present an analysis framework and instructor tool that leverage LLMs to classify, cluster, and present students' coding errors in real time. The approach uses a prompt-engineered GPT-4o agent to classify syntactical, conceptual, and strategic errors, then clusters them via Universal Sentence Encoder embeddings + KMeans, achieving 89.5% error-classification agreement in a pilot study.
papers.relevance: Provides a validated LLM-based error classification and clustering pipeline that can be adapted from real-time lecture use to offline analysis of archived autograder submission logs, directly feeding the misconception taxonomy DT-2 agenda.

additionalRefs.title: Keuning, Jeuring & Heeren (2019): A Systematic Literature Review of Automated Feedback Generation for Programming Exercises
additionalRefs.authors: Hieke Keuning, Johan Jeuring, Bastiaan Heeren
additionalRefs.relevance: Comprehensive survey of 66 automated feedback tools; establishes baseline taxonomy of feedback types (errors reported, hints, explanations) and identifies misconception-targeted feedback as underserved but high-impact.

additionalRefs.title: Qian & Lehman (2017): Students' Misconceptions and Other Difficulties in Introductory Programming
additionalRefs.relevance: Canonical reference for CS1 misconception taxonomy covering variable scope, loops, conditionals, and object identity. Used by the SIGCSE 2026 paper as the classification schema — gives empirical grounding for the cluster labels.

additionalRefs.title: Price, Dong & Lipovac (2017): iSnap: Towards Intelligent Tutoring in a Novice Programming Environment
additionalRefs.authors: Thomas W. Price, Yihuan Dong, Dragan Lipovac
additionalRefs.relevance: Shows that hint systems grounded in common-mistake patterns produce measurable learning gains; provides methodological precedent for the A/B evaluation design.

researchPlan.overview: This project constructs a misconception taxonomy from archived Jolly Feedback submission logs using the SIGCSE 2026 LLM-classification approach, then builds a targeted LLM critique layer that ties feedback to specific misconceptions. The evaluation tests whether misconception-targeted feedback reduces resubmission cycles in CSS 142 compared to plain pass/fail output — a clean A/B comparison on infrastructure already owned.

milestones.deliverable: Annotated Qian & Lehman taxonomy extended with C++/Java-specific patterns; replication of SIGCSE 2026 classification pipeline on 200-error sample from Jolly Feedback logs

milestones.goal: Full log analysis and cluster construction
milestones.deliverable: LLM classification run on full Jolly Feedback archive; KMeans clusters reviewed and labeled; final 20-30 misconception category taxonomy document
Prompt library: one critique template per taxonomy category; outputs explanation of WHY the error reflects the misconception + conceptual next step, without revealing code
Extended Jolly Feedback that routes each test failure through the misconception classifier and attaches a targeted LLM critique to the email report; deployed to sandbox section
Submission-log comparison: resubmission rate and time-to-pass for targeted vs. standard feedback groups in CSS 142 (using existing system logs, no new human-subjects protocol needed)
Draft paper with RQ, method, results, and discussion submitted to SIGCSE or ICER

researchPlan.resources: Existing Jolly Feedback submission logs from CSS 142 (C++/Python); Claude API (Sonnet tier) for classification and critique generation; GitHub Actions for pipeline integration; no new course infrastructure needed.

risks.risk: Archived logs may not have enough volume per assignment to reach statistical significance in the evaluation
risks.mitigation: Extend data collection over two academic terms; use effect-size framing if n is modest, and position as a feasibility study with a clearly-stated future replication plan

risks.risk: LLM misconception classifier may not generalize from Python (training domain) to C++ submission patterns
risks.mitigation: Start with 200-error human-validated sample to measure cross-language accuracy before scaling; adapt few-shot examples to C++ idioms

risks.risk: Misconception-targeted feedback may leak solution strategies if prompts are not carefully constrained
risks.mitigation: Add explicit 'do not reveal code or algorithm' constraint to all critique prompts; blind human rater review of 50 outputs before deployment
